S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report any thermal event involving fire, smoke, injury, emergency-service response, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, with a preliminary incident report. Manufacturers must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk, and report aggregate model-level incident counts to regulators quarterly.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Manufacturers must provide per-model results to the regulator and disclose them to customers who buy that model; results must identify the model, test date and protocol, sample size, and failures. Per-model failure rates are not required to be published to the general public. No more than 10% of tested units for any model may fail; exceeding 10% requires prompt regulator review and appropriate protective action, which may include a stop-sale or recall based on the evidence.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: Newly installed systems must include a remote emergency shut-off function no later than 12 months after adoption. Manufacturers must provide a secure software or hardware retrofit enabling remote shut-off for installed units within 72 months after adoption, where technically feasible, and report progress and exceptions to the regulator annually.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: All new home battery systems must include built-in fire suppression no later than 36 months after adoption. Regulators may grant a time-limited, publicly documented extension where a manufacturer demonstrates that compliant suppression is not yet technically available, without waiving other fire-safety requirements.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: If a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any rolling 12-month period, based on regulator-validated reports, the manufacturer must notify the regulator within 24 hours and submit a risk assessment and corrective-action plan within 10 calendar days. The regulator must promptly assess whether a recall or other protective action is necessary, considering incident severity, trend, and available risk controls; it may require a recall or stop-sale at any time where evidence indicates an imminent serious risk.

document.section_notes: The final standard sets a 10% permanent per-model failure ceiling in S2, with no mandatory stop-sale, and per-model results go to purchasers and regulators but not the public, which protects Northwind's Hearth 10 (6.2%). S5 makes recall discretionary with no numeric mandatory trigger, which protects Halcyon's Ember 8 (9.9/100k), while S4's 36-month suppression deadline favours Halcyon's cost position. S1 is strong and all parameters are safe. The S4 extension clause is noted but was not treated as changing the 36-month requirement.
